title: Direct Lake: Import-Speed Analytics Without the Copy
summary: Direct Lake is a Power BI semantic model storage mode that reads Delta tables straight from OneLake — delivering import-like query speed without moving data and DirectQuery-like freshness without a separate cache. This article covers how it works, the two storage-mode flavors, framing and lazy loading, performance internals, and the patterns and pitfalls every practitioner needs to know.
body_md:
## What Is Direct Lake and Why Should You Care?

Direct Lake is a semantic-model storage mode in which a Power BI model reads Delta tables straight from OneLake, avoiding both data import and DirectQuery, and so pairs import-like performance with DirectQuery-like freshness [S1]. In the Analysis Services engine that underpins Power BI, Direct Lake lets semantic models read Delta Parquet data directly from OneLake without maintaining a copied dataset, sitting alongside the existing Import and DirectQuery modes [S2]. For report builders, this translates to queries against data sitting in OneLake without importing it into the model or keeping a separate cache [S3].

Before Direct Lake, practitioners faced a hard trade-off: Import mode is fast but goes stale and requires scheduled refreshes that copy potentially large datasets; DirectQuery is always fresh but adds SQL round-trip latency to every visual render. Direct Lake dissolves that trade-off. The Parquet files that Fabric lakehouses and warehouses already write to OneLake become the live source for Power BI, with no secondary copy to maintain.

## Two Flavors: Direct Lake on OneLake vs. Direct Lake on SQL

Direct Lake comes in two storage-mode variants [S6]:

- **Direct Lake on OneLake** — the model's shared expression points straight at the OneLake storage location. OneLake APIs handle schema discovery, security checks, and data loading with no SQL analytics endpoint involved [S6]. This flavor offers OneLake security, richer modelling features, and faster query performance [S4].
- **Direct Lake on SQL** — the shared expression points at the SQL analytics endpoint, which is consulted only for schema and security discovery; actual data is still read directly from OneLake unless a query falls back to DirectQuery [S6]. This flavor is the right choice when SQL analytics endpoint security rules are needed under delegated identity, or when DirectQuery fallback is required [S4].

Power BI Desktop and the Power BI service create only Direct Lake on OneLake models. The SQL analytics endpoint page is the creation path that offers a choice between both flavors [S6]. When creating a model from the SQL analytics endpoint, the type dialog defaults to Direct Lake on OneLake if the endpoint runs in user identity mode, and to Direct Lake on SQL if it runs in delegated identity mode [S6].

![Direct Lake query path vs DirectQuery fallback](/content/diagrams/direct-lake-query-path.svg)

## How Direct Lake Works: Lazy Loading and Framing

Direct Lake loads column data from OneLake lazily: nothing is read until a query first touches a column, and the load set includes not just the columns a query names but also those needed by relationships and measures [S5]. When a report visual requests data from a Direct Lake table, the semantic model reads the Delta table in OneLake directly and may retain recently accessed data in an in-memory cache to serve subsequent queries efficiently [S8].

The diagram below traces what happens underneath that lazy load: how a column moves through the cold/semiwarm/warm/hot residency ladder, how row groups transcode into VertiPaq segments, what triggers framing and eviction, and how the DirectQuery fallback decision plays out for each storage flavor.

![Original diagram: Direct Lake internals — column residency lifecycle (cold/semiwarm/warm/hot) with cold-query transcoding, row-group-to-segment mapping, framing and eviction triggers, and the DirectQuery fallback decision tree by storage flavor](/diagrams/direct-lake-internals.svg)

### Framing: Metadata-Only Snapshots

Framing is the mechanism by which a Direct Lake model binds itself to a point-in-time view of the Delta table. A framing operation is metadata-only and typically finishes in seconds: the model reads the latest Delta table version and rebinds itself to the current Parquet file set, establishing the new baseline for future column loading [S5].

Direct Lake queries reflect the Delta table state as of the most recent successful framing operation, not the live table, so writes landing after the last frame remain invisible until the next one [S5]. An automatic-updates model setting — on by default — reframes Direct Lake tables whenever the underlying OneLake data changes; turn it off to control data visibility through manual or scheduled framing [S5].

Framing can fail when a Delta table breaches capacity guardrails, such as exceeding 10,000 Parquet files in a single table [S5].

### DirectQuery Fallback (Direct Lake on SQL Only)

DirectQuery fallback exists only in Direct Lake on SQL. Documented triggers include querying a SQL analytics endpoint view, querying a table with SQL-endpoint row-level security, and a Delta table exceeding capacity guardrails [S5]. A fallen-back query reads the SQL analytics endpoint directly and therefore returns the latest data, escaping the framing point-in-time — at the cost of typically slower performance [S5].

Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back to DirectQuery and skips SQL-endpoint coupling entirely, which enables more efficient DAX query plans since no SQL security check is needed [S5]. Fallback behavior for Direct Lake on SQL models is governed by the model's `DirectLakeBehavior` property; this property has no effect on Direct Lake on OneLake models [S5].

A Direct Lake on SQL table can fall back to DirectQuery through the SQL analytics endpoint when Direct Lake mode cannot be used, and this fallback is governed by the model's Direct Lake behavior property [S8].

## Developing Direct Lake Models

Direct Lake models can be developed beyond the browser with XMLA-compliant tools such as SSMS 19.1+, community tools, or programmatically from Fabric notebooks via semantic link and semantic-link-labs [S6].

You can identify a model's Direct Lake flavor from its M expression in TMDL view: Direct Lake on OneLake uses the Azure Data Lake Storage connector, while Direct Lake on SQL uses the SQL Server or OneLake.SqlAnalytics connector [S6].

Over XMLA, a Direct Lake model is recognizable by a database `compatibilityLevel` of 1604 or higher, partitions whose mode is `directLake`, and partitions that reference a shared expression as their data source [S6].

## Best Practices

**Use Direct Lake on OneLake as your default.** It delivers OneLake security, more modelling features, and faster query performance [S4]. Reserve Direct Lake on SQL only when SQL analytics endpoint security or DirectQuery fallback is a hard requirement [S4].

**Control framing for in-flight ETL.** Pinning queries to a framing point is useful when Delta data is transient — for example, mid-ETL. Disabling automatic updates and framing deliberately yields consistent results during long-running loads [S5].

**Use low-cardinality partition columns.** Partition Delta tables only on low-cardinality columns (Microsoft suggests staying under about 100–200 distinct values). Over-partitioning multiplies small Parquet files and row groups, inflating segment counts in the model and degrading query performance [S7].

**Target larger Parquet files.** A 1 GB BinSize target is recommended when writing Delta tables that back Power BI Direct Lake semantic models, because larger files align with the Direct Lake loading pattern and reduce the number of segment loads needed [S10].

**Check network settings before deploying.** Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active. Semantic models relying on Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints, making this connection mode incompatible with the most restrictive Fabric network isolation posture [S9].

## What Goes Wrong

**SQL views force DirectQuery fallback.** Basing a Direct Lake on SQL model table on a SQL view forces every query against that table into DirectQuery fallback, which usually slows it down. Prefer base tables for Direct Lake mode [S6].

**Overwrite operations defeat incremental framing.** Loading a Delta table with the Overwrite option wipes the table's commit history. This defeats incremental framing and forces a full cold-state reload of all segments, dictionaries, and join indexes on the next query [S7].

**Vacuuming too aggressively breaks queries.** A framed Direct Lake model is pinned to a specific Delta commit version. Vacuuming must not remove the Parquet files of that version before the next reframe, or user queries fail when the referenced files are gone [S7].

## Performance and Internals

Direct Lake models occupy one of four memory-residency states — cold, semiwarm, warm, or hot — with query latency improving at each step. The hot state adds populated VertiScan caches on top of fully resident column data [S7].

On a cold-state query, Direct Lake must merge the per-row-group local Parquet dictionaries of each needed column into a single global VertiPaq dictionary. A Delta table with more row groups therefore takes longer to transcode [S7]. Answering a cold multi-table DAX query also requires Direct Lake to build join indexes from relationship key columns (loading their dictionaries plus the one-side key segments) and to load any Delta deletion vectors so deleted rows are excluded [S7].

Transcoding is usually a direct remap of Parquet data IDs to VertiPaq IDs when both sides use RLE/Bit-Packing hybrid encoding. If a Parquet file used plain or delta encoding instead, Direct Lake must re-encode the values, which slows column loading [S7].

V-Order speeds Direct Lake in two ways: it raises RLE compression quality so columns stream into memory faster during transcoding, and it lets VertiScan compute results directly on compressed data without a decompression step [S7].

The total row-group count across a Delta table's Parquet files maps one-to-one to the number of VertiPaq segments per model column. Many tiny row groups produce many tiny column segments and degrade query performance [S7]. For large tables Direct Lake prefers column segments of roughly 1 to 16 million rows. Row groups well under 1 million rows hurt performance [S7].

During incremental framing, Direct Lake reads each table's Delta log and evicts only the column segments tied to removed row groups, while dictionaries are kept and merely extended with new values to avoid re-transcoding [S7].

Direct Lake does not use Delta or Parquet statistics for row-group or file skipping when loading column data, so pruning optimizations that help other engines do not reduce its transcoding work [S7].

A resident column can be evicted for three reasons: a framing operation after the source Delta table changed, prolonged non-use by queries, or general memory pressure on the capacity from concurrent operations [S5].

## Worked Example

Consider a data engineering team that loads daily sales data from an external system into a Fabric lakehouse. The ingestion pipeline writes new Parquet files to the lakehouse's Delta table using Optimized Write, targeting a 1 GB BinSize [S10]. The Delta table is partitioned by `sales_region`, a column with 12 distinct values — well within the 100–200 value guidance [S7].

The semantic model is created as Direct Lake on OneLake from the Power BI service, with automatic updates enabled [S6]. As each pipeline run completes, framing triggers automatically and rebinds the model to the new Delta commit version within seconds [S5]. Report users see fresh data with no scheduled dataset refresh.

*Inference:* The team can optionally disable automatic updates during a multi-step ETL that writes intermediate states to the same table, manually triggering framing only when all steps complete — ensuring report users never see partial results.

For the security team, because the model uses Direct Lake on OneLake rather than Direct Lake on SQL, OneLake workspace roles govern data access directly, and no SQL analytics endpoint row-level security is needed [S6]. The team ensures the network posture does not activate Block Public Internet Access, which would sever the Direct Lake connection [S9].
